clinicalPearls: The M-type phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R1) is the dominant podocyte autoantigen in primary membranous nephropathy, accounting for the large majority of cases.
Circulating anti-PLA2R autoantibodies are predominantly of the IgG4 subclass and serve as a diagnostic, prognostic and monitoring biomarker.
In the right clinical context, seropositivity with a compatible presentation can support the diagnosis and, in selected patients, may permit deferral of biopsy.
Enhanced glomerular PLA2R antigen staining on biopsy can be positive even when serum antibody is undetectable, improving diagnostic sensitivity.

Antibody level broadly tracks disease activity: immunological remission (falling titre) typically precedes clinical remission of proteinuria, and persistent or rising titres predict progression or relapse.
The nephrotic state carries a high thromboembolic risk, including renal vein thrombosis, warranting vigilance and prophylaxis considerations.
Seropositivity does not exclude a secondary cause; malignancy, hepatitis B, lupus and certain drugs must still be considered, particularly with atypical features.
Antibody-guided immunosuppression, commonly B-cell depletion with rituximab, has become central to management of higher-risk disease.
reference.pathophysiology: PLA2R1 is a large type-I transmembrane glycoprotein of the mannose-receptor family constitutively expressed on the apical surface of podocytes. In primary membranous nephropathy, autoantibodies recognise conformation-dependent epitopes within the cysteine-rich (ricin-B) domain and the C-type lectin domains of the receptor. These antibodies bind PLA2R in situ on the podocyte, forming subepithelial immune deposits along the outer aspect of the glomerular basement membrane. Although IgG4 is a poor activator of the classical complement pathway, complement activation, chiefly via the lectin and alternative pathways, generates the C5b-9 membrane-attack complex sublytically on the podocyte. This drives cytoskeletal derangement, foot-process effacement, oxidative and endoplasmic-reticulum stress, and shedding of podocytes, producing the characteristic non-selective proteinuria. Progressive deposit formation with intervening basement-membrane spikes yields the thickened capillary walls seen histologically, while ongoing antigen-antibody interaction sustains injury until the autoimmune response abates spontaneously or with therapy.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary membranous nephropathy (malignancy, hepatitis B or C, systemic lupus erythematosus class V, drugs)
THSD7A-associated membranous nephropathy and other rarer antigen types
Minimal-change disease and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
Renal amyloidosis and monoclonal deposition disease
additionalInvestigations: Serum anti-PLA2R antibody by immunofluorescence assay and/or ELISA, with serial titres for monitoring
Renal biopsy with PLA2R antigen immunostaining, IgG subclass mapping and electron microscopy
THSD7A antibody and antigen testing when PLA2R is negative
Hepatitis B and C serology and autoimmune/complement panel
Quantification of proteinuria and assessment of kidney function over time
Evaluation of thromboembolic risk including serum albumin trend
redFlags: Declining kidney function or refractory nephrotic-range proteinuria
Thromboembolic events such as renal vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism
Features suggesting an underlying malignancy or other secondary cause
Very high or persistently rising anti-PLA2R titres despite therapy
Rapid deterioration suggesting superimposed crescentic or anti-GBM disease
reference.prognosis: Outcomes follow a broad spectrum historically summarised as roughly a third achieving spontaneous remission, a third with persistent proteinuria and a third progressing; antibody status now refines this, with low or falling titres favouring remission and high, persistent titres predicting progression and guiding treatment intensity.
pitfalls: Assuming PLA2R positivity excludes a secondary cause and omitting malignancy or viral screening
Treating on biopsy appearance alone without measuring or monitoring antibody titres
Neglecting thromboembolic prophylaxis in profound nephrotic hypoalbuminaemia
Missing seronegative disease where only tissue antigen staining is positive
Failing to test for THSD7A and other antigens when PLA2R is negative
references: International clinical practice guideline on glomerular diseases
Reference review on membranous nephropathy antigens and serology
management: Begin supportive antiproteinuric and antihypertensive therapy with renin-angiotensin system blockade, dietary sodium restriction, statins and diuretics for oedema
Reserve immunosuppression for high-risk or persistent nephrotic disease, using rituximab (anti-CD20) as preferred first-line therapy
Consider a calcineurin inhibitor or a cyclical corticosteroid-alkylating agent (Ponticelli) regimen as alternative immunosuppression
Provide thromboprophylaxis or therapeutic anticoagulation given the high venous and renal-vein thrombosis risk of the nephrotic state
Monitor serial anti-PLA2R antibody titres to guide immunosuppression and detect relapse, tracking proteinuria and kidney function
Screen for secondary contributors including hepatitis B and C and age-appropriate malignancy
Escalate or intensify immunosuppression when antibody titres persist or rise, under nephrology supervision
Update vaccinations and take infection precautions before starting immunosuppression
